documents.name: CS301 Lecture 6 - Normalization.pdf
documents.content: A functional dependency X -> Y holds in a relation when every pair of tuples that agree on X also agree on Y. Functional dependencies are the formal basis for normalization. A relation is in second normal form (2NF) if it is in first normal form and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key; that is, there are no partial dependencies. A relation is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is stricter: for every non-trivial dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey. Decomposition into BCNF is always lossless-join but may not be dependency-preserving. When dependency preservation is essential, designers often settle for 3NF, which guarantees both lossless join and dependency preservation.

documents.name: CS305 Lecture 4 - CPU Scheduling.pdf
documents.content: First-Come First-Served (FCFS) scheduling runs processes in arrival order. It is simple but suffers from the convoy effect, where short processes wait behind a long one. Shortest Job First (SJF) selects the process with the smallest next CPU burst and is provably optimal for minimizing average waiting time, but it requires knowledge of future burst lengths, which is usually estimated with exponential averaging of previous bursts. Round-robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time quantum. A very small quantum increases context-switch overhead, whereas a very large quantum degenerates into FCFS. A quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds is typical. Multilevel feedback queues allow processes to move between queues based on their observed CPU usage, favouring interactive processes while still guaranteeing progress for long-running jobs.
